sections.html:
• Common name: African clawed frog (also African claw-toad frog, common platanna)
  • Scientific name: Xenopus laevis
  • Minimum tank: 10 gallons (40 litres)
  • Breeding: medium to difficult
  • KH: 4–12
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: carnivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Life span: up to 20 years
  • Colour: from olive green to grey; albino form exists

In the aquarium hobby the African clawed frog is often confused with and mislabelled as the African dwarf frog or "dwarf African clawed frog". It is extremely important not to make this mistake. African clawed frogs are voracious predators; there are documented reports of them attacking and killing prey, such as fish, even larger than themselves, tearing it apart with their powerful clawed hind feet. They also eat other frog species.

Although the two are similar in appearance, they can be told apart:

  • African clawed frogs have eyes on top of the head; African dwarf frogs have eyes on the sides.
  • African clawed frogs have flat snouts; African dwarf frogs have pointed snouts.
  • African clawed frogs have webbed hind feet and free digits on the forefeet; African dwarf frogs have webbed fore and hind feet.
African dwarf frog (Hymenochirus boettgeri)African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis)

Be very careful in pet stores: they may look similar when small, but this mistake can lead to a massacre in a peaceful community tank.

The frog is readily available in local pet stores and online from reputable breeders. Signs of a healthy frog are smooth skin, a flattened body, clear eyes and activity. Avoid lethargic frogs, which are passive and unwilling to eat.

The African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis) is an African aquatic frog of the family Pipidae, a family of primitive, toothless, entirely aquatic frogs. The genus Xenopus is indigenous to sub-Saharan Africa and comprises twenty species; the most popular are Xenopus laevis and Xenopus tropicalis (western or tropical clawed frog).

Its native range includes Angola, Cameroon, Congo, Kenya, Namibia, Nigeria, South Africa, Sudan, Uganda, Zambia, etc. As an invasive species it has been introduced to other parts of the world, including Chile, France, Mexico, the United States and the United Kingdom.

This aquatic frog inhabits the shallow rivers, ponds and lakes of sub-Saharan Africa, in both arid and semi-arid climates.

It is tolerant of changes in its environment and will survive in almost any body of water. It is also capable of aestivation during dry periods, migrating to new habitats, and surviving in waters with high salinity.

A 10-gallon (40 litre) tank is the minimum for housing one or two African clawed frogs. Since this frog is an excellent escape artist, fit the aquarium with a secure lid.

Keep the water depth around 17–30 cm, which gives ample space for swimming and lets the frog reach the surface at intervals to breathe.

Although this frog thrives in still or stagnant water in nature, it should not be kept in unclean water in captivity. Carry out partial weekly water changes (25%) to keep the water clean.

The body of the African clawed frog is slimy due to mucus secretion, which makes it very slippery. It is best to avoid handling the frogs unless there is an important reason. Ideally use gloves; do not touch them with bare hands unless there is no option. If you must, clean your hands first and grip the frog properly to prevent it slipping.

• Temperature: 20–25 °C.
  • pH: optimal between 6.5 and 8.0.
  • Hardness: 5–20 GH.

The frog is tolerant of environmental changes, but good water quality helps keep it healthy and disease-free. Water should be dechlorinated before use; a water conditioner (such as Seachem Prime) can be used, or the water can be left to stand for at least 24 hours.

Lighting: a normal LED aquarium light is fine; special UVB light is not required. Provide a 12/12 light cycle (12 hours on, 12 hours off), which can be set with a timer, to mimic natural light and dark periods. If there are plants in the tank, adapt the lighting to the plants' needs.

Substrate: use medium or large gravel and avoid small grains or pebbles, because the frog may accidentally swallow them. Small gravel in the gut can cause severe injuries and even death, so choose gravel that cannot fit into the frog's mouth.

Decor: provide plenty of hiding places using caves, rocks, pipes and hollow wood. Strong live plants such as Anubias and Java fern, which do not need a nutrient-rich substrate, can also be used. The frogs appreciate the hiding places the decor provides.

Filtration: a good filtration system is essential, but because the frogs are very sensitive to movement and vibrations in the water, avoid powerful filters that make the water turbulent and stress the frogs.

In the larval stage, African clawed frogs filter-feed on plankton in the water. Adults actively scavenge for dead insects and pieces of organic waste, and also eat live tadpoles, worms, crustaceans, snails, small fish and any other organism within reach.

In captivity they can be fed a variety of foods: bloodworms, waxworms, tubifex worms, shrimp, grubs, feeder fish and commercially prepared amphibian food.

Feed a varied diet daily and monitor the frog's size. If it looks overweight, feed every other day; if it looks too slim and unhealthy, feed more often. Frogs stop eating once full, and uneaten food should then be removed. Do not overfeed; it is better to give small portions that they finish quickly.

If a frog is not feeding well, try feeding it directly with tweezers. After a while it may become accustomed to this and reach for food when it sees it coming.

In the wild, African clawed frogs migrate to nearby water bodies during droughts, or burrow into the mud and become dormant for up to a year, re-emerging only when conditions are favourable again.

They are voracious eaters, taking tadpoles, fry, worms and more. They are aroused by the scent of food, alive or dead, and swim around in search of it until they grasp it. Catching prey is easy thanks to their extremely sensitive fingers, acute sense of smell and a lateral line system that senses movement and vibrations in the water.

The short forelimbs direct food to the mouth, while the muscular hind limbs mainly propel the frog through the water. Since they have no tongue, they rely on the forelimbs for feeding. They use the three short claws on each hind limb to shred large pieces of food, and occasionally to dig worms, food particles and organic matter out of the mud.

Tankmates: African clawed frogs are aggressive, very persistent predators with a great appetite. They are omnivorous and can easily hunt small and medium-sized fish, so keeping them with small fish, dwarf shrimp or freshwater snails is not recommended. Keeping them with large fish is also undesirable, as the fish may bite off their fingers. It is recommended to keep them separately in a species-only tank. One female and several males can live together, but individuals should be matched to a similar size because of the frogs' tendency to cannibalism.

Males and females are easily distinguished.

  • Males are smaller than females.
  • Males have slim bodies and legs, while females are bigger and plumper.
  • Males also develop black nuptial pads on their forearms, which help them clasp the female during amplexus.

Reproductive behaviour can be induced by simulating spring rain: lower the water temperature to 18–20 °C for 4 to 6 weeks and reduce the water level to 10–15 cm. Carry out partial water changes during this period. Afterwards, top up the water and raise the temperature to 25–28 °C for 1–2 weeks, with the lights turned off.

The male signals readiness to mate with a metallic clicking call, and the female answers with a matching click. The male then grasps the receptive female just above the hind legs (inguinal amplexus). The pair moves in a circular motion until all the eggs are laid (up to hundreds), and the male fertilises them. This can last from 2 hours to 2 days. The female lays 200 eggs or more, and incubation lasts 3–7 days depending on temperature.

Hatching and tadpoles: adults devour their own eggs, so place the eggs in a separate tank with clean, dechlorinated fresh water at 26–28 °C; they hatch in 2–4 days. After hatching the tadpoles hang on plants and other objects, attached by the secretion of special glands. On the 3rd–4th day the tadpole's muzzle becomes wedge-shaped and long tactile threads appear at the corners of the mouth. Tadpoles start feeding on the 7th day by filtering micro-organisms from the water, transform into froglets within 2 months and reach maturity at 16–24 months.

The African clawed frog is widely used as a model organism for biological and biochemical studies, and was the first vertebrate cloned in a laboratory, in 1962. In nature it lives about 15 years; in captivity up to 20 years, and under optimal conditions there are reports of up to 30 years.

Description: a dull-coloured aquatic frog with three short claws on each hind limb, used to shred large food. The eyes have no eyelids and sit on top of a wedge-shaped head. The forelimbs are small and unwebbed; the hind limbs are large, muscular and webbed. Cartilaginous tympanic discs beside the eyes aid hearing, since there are no external eardrums. The body is smooth, slimy and flattened, typically grey to olive green with brown or dark grey spots on the back and limbs, with a pale yellow or off-white underside. Adults are usually 12–14 cm.

Health problems:

  • Dropsy (oedema): severe bloating of the abdomen and legs, mostly caused by abnormal fluid accumulation from improper metabolism, which puts extreme pressure on the vital organs. Take the sick frog to an expert to release the fluids. Other causes of bloat include internal bacterial infections, poor diet and ingestion of gravel or rocks; bloat from bacterial infection can be treated with Maracyn Plus.
  • Red leg: caused by the bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila (gram-negative). Symptoms are red, swollen legs, which can worsen until the skin of the legs rots off. Contact a vet.
  • Fungal infections: the frogs are easy targets of Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, the fungus that causes amphibian chytridiomycosis. Quarantine the infected frog to prevent spread and treat it with Mardel Maroxy anti-fungal solution. Methylene blue can also be used, as a tank treatment or dip.

Keep the water clean at all times and keep to a good feeding schedule to prevent the build-up of harmful toxins and microbes. If a frog shows problems, remove it to a separate tank and consult a professional vet.
